public_sources.observed_claim: Azure LLM traces: output-length coefficient of variation 3.30 for code and 1.50 for conversation; long-tailed inputs and bursty arrivals also reported.
public_sources.use: sets two synthetic rollout-latency tail-shape stress levels only; not treated as a latency calibration

public_sources.observed_claim: LLM serving has extreme length variability; P90-P99 tail latency is decision-relevant and distribution-aware scheduling reduced P99 TTLT by up to 35-50% in the reported workloads.
public_sources.use: supports evaluating tail rather than mean and testing scheduler sensitivity

public_sources.observed_claim: Sarathi-Serve identifies batching/prefill-decode interference as a throughput-latency tradeoff and uses stall-free schedules to add requests without pausing ongoing decodes.
public_sources.use: supports treating synchronous batch barriers versus refill scheduling as a real systems design dimension

public_sources.observed_claim: Rare stragglers can dominate fan-out latency; hedged/tied requests and cancellation can reduce tail latency with modest extra work in the paper's Google examples.
public_sources.use: motivates explicit straggler and cancellation sensitivity; synthetic 1% x10 stress is not an empirical estimate from this source

tested_latency_model.purpose: source-explicit stress surrogate, not calibrated deployment prediction
tested_latency_model.baseline_policy: five (r=20,k=16) candidate audits followed by fifteen (r=50,k=36) audits; rho_discordance=0.20; candidate stages serial
tested_latency_model.rollout_time_marginal: lognormal with median normalized to 1 and CV matching source-reported output-length CV
tested_latency_model.synchronous: launch b pairs; wait for whole batch; final partial batch rounded up to b and paid in full
tested_latency_model.asynchronous_cancel: keep b pair jobs in flight; refill a pair slot immediately when its pair completes; once the statistical stopping boundary is reached, stop launches and cancel in-flight pairs
tested_latency_model.async_validity_assumption: conditional on prelaunch covariates and past, pair completion time/order is ignorable for the paired sign; equivalently null sign symmetry remains valid after conditioning on completion-time filtration

latency_results.units: wall in normalized median-rollout-time units; occupancy is sum of candidate+incumbent runtime in the same normalized units
summary: Under latency/sign ignorability, asynchronous refill+cancellation reduced q95 wall time by 56.2-85.6% in the conversation-like stress and 70.0-95.3% in the code-like+straggler stress versus synchronous full-batch barriers.
With effective cancellation, q95 consumed rollout occupancy also fell by 1.5-11.6% and 9.7-35.9%, respectively.
If cancellation does not actually release paid work, async full-obligation q95 occupancy was about 1.0-10.1% above synchronous while retaining the wall-time gain.
These are stress-model results, not measured production speedups.

resource_price_tradeoff.objective: J = q95_wall + lambda * q95_full_obligation_rollout_occupancy for asynchronous refill when cancellation is ineffective
resource_price_tradeoff.scope: lambda has units of wall-time penalty per rollout-occupancy unit; peak reserved concurrency price and queue interference are not included

completion_order_validity_stress.construction: all-null launch stream has marginal P(+|discordant)=P(-|discordant)=0.5 and rho=0.2, but exponential pair latency is multiplied by a sign-specific factor. Async consumes signs in completion order and stops/cancels at the exact-curtailment boundary.
completion_order_validity_stress.result: Completion-order async is not automatically measurement-valid. Even though the launch-order marginal sign null is exactly symmetric, sign-dependent latency makes the observed completion-order sign stream selective; larger concurrency can amplify the distortion.
completion_order_validity_stress.required_gate: Before using completion-order refill/cancellation for a decision-critical paired sign test, establish conditional sign symmetry/latency ignorability or use a reveal/inclusion order fixed independently of completion latency.

rejected_or_narrowed_generalizations: Rejected: statistical validity is automatically preserved when only the scheduler changes and the marginal launch-order sign null remains 50/50.

Rejected: cancellation is merely a systems optimization with no measurement consequence; if cancellation/inclusion depends on completion order and latency correlates with sign, FWER can exceed its certificate.
Narrowed: very large async wall gains are specific to the synthetic heavy-tail model and synchronous full-batch baseline, not a production performance claim.
Narrowed: effective cancellation occupancy dominance does not account for peak reserved GPU slots, queueing externalities, model-side batching interactions, or cancellation granularity.

frontier.action: Design a latency-safe scheduler that preassigns launch/reveal priority independently of outcomes and completion times, then quantify how much of the async wall gain survives head-of-line blocking; compare fixed launch-order reveal, random-priority reveal and bounded reorder-window variants.

Instrument or obtain actual paired candidate/incumbent rollout latency traces with task id, prelaunch covariates, completion times and paired outcome, then directly test conditional sign-latency dependence before deploying completion-order cancellation.
Add peak concurrency price, independent-side candidate/incumbent slot reuse, queue interference and cancellation latency to the wall/occupancy objective.
After the validity gate is resolved, rerun the full globally-certified action frontier rather than only the fixed five-(20,16)+fifteen-(50,36) baseline.

exact_next_action: Construct a precommitted reveal-order asynchronous scheduler whose statistical inclusion order is independent of completion latency, derive its null-validity argument, and simulate q95 wall/occupancy under the same CV=1.5 and CV=3.3+straggler stress models to measure the price of validity relative to completion-order async.
